prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

She awoke to find her fishtail clean gone but in the bed with her were two long, cold thingammies. You'd have thought they were tangles of kelp or collops of ham. "They're no doubt taking the piss, it being New Year's Eve. Half the staff legless with drink and the other half playing pranks. Still, this is taking it a bit far." And with that she hurled the two thingammies out of the room. But here's the thing she still doesn't get— why she tumbled out after them arse-over-tip... How she was connected to those two thingammies and how they were connected to her. It was the sister who gave her the wink and let her know what was what. "You have one leg attached to you there and another one underneath that. One leg, two legs... A-one and a-two... Now you have to learn what they can do." In the long months that followed, I wonder if her heart fell the way her arches fell, her instep arches.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: She, You, They

outputs.L1:
She awoke to find her fishtail clean gone, and in the bed beside her lay two long, cold thingammies. You might have taken them for tangles of kelp or collops of ham.

“They’re no doubt taking the piss, it being New Year’s Eve. Half the staff are legless with drink, and the other half are playing pranks. Still, this is taking things a bit far.”

And with that, she hurled the two thingammies out of the room. But here’s the thing she still doesn’t understand: why she tumbled out after them, arse-over-tip; how she was connected to those two thingammies, and how they were connected to her.

It was the sister who gave her the wink and let her know what was what. “You have one leg attached to you there, and another one underneath that. One leg, two legs... A-one and a-two... Now you have to learn what they can do.”

In the long months that followed, I wonder whether her heart fell as her arches fell—her instep arches.
outputs.L2:
When she came to, her fish’s tail had vanished entirely. In its place, stretched beneath the covers, were a pair of long, chilly whatsits—things that might have been twisted seaweed or thick slices of ham.

“It must be a New Year’s Eve joke,” she thought. “Half the workers are too drunk to stand, and the rest are up to mischief. But this prank has gone well beyond the limit.”

So she flung both strange objects out through the doorway. What continued to baffle her was why she immediately pitched after them, tumbling head over heels. She had no idea that the two things belonged to her, or that she belonged with them.

A sister finally clued her in with a knowing look. “That’s one leg fixed to you there, and there’s another below it. First leg, second leg—one, then two. Now you must discover how to use them.”

During the many months afterward, I can’t help wondering whether her spirits sank along with the arches of her new feet.
outputs.L3:
She wakes on New Year’s morning to discover that her familiar fishtail has vanished. In its place are two long, unfamiliar legs. Convinced that the strange limbs must be part of an elaborate New Year’s Eve prank, she grabs them and attempts to throw them out of the room. To her shock, she tumbles after them, not yet realizing that they are attached to her body.

One of her sisters soon comes to her aid and gently explains what has happened: she now has two legs, and she will have to learn how to use them. The adjustment is neither quick nor easy. Over the following months, she struggles to stand, balance, and walk, while also grappling with the emotional consequences of losing the body she once knew. Gradually, through repeated effort, frustration, and support from those around her, she begins to adapt to her transformed life.
outputs.L4:
When Mira awoke, the sea was gone.

She lay on a bed of wet stones beneath a pale morning sky. Waves reached toward her and slipped back, leaving ribbons of foam around her body. She tried to lift her tail, expecting the familiar weight of silver-green scales, but nothing answered.

In its place were two long, colorless things.

They bent in the middle and ended in narrow shapes fringed with small, curling pieces. Mira cried out. The unfamiliar limbs twitched at the sound, and their movement frightened her even more. She seized one with both hands. It was warm and soft, jointed like the legs of a crab but without a shell. When she pinched it, pain flashed through her.

Still, she could not believe the things belonged to her.

A storm must have thrown some land creature against her, she decided. Perhaps these were remains tangled beneath her body. She gripped them behind the knees and dragged herself toward a hollow between the rocks. Each pull sent fire through her hips, yet fear made her strong. With one final effort, she pushed both legs into the hollow and covered them with strips of seaweed.

At once she collapsed.

The hidden limbs lay several paces away, but the pain remained. Worse, she could feel the cold stones beneath feet she could no longer see. When a crab crawled over one of her buried toes, she screamed.

Her sister Neris rose from the water a moment later.

She pulled herself onto the shore, her dark blue tail beating anxiously against the rocks. “Mira!”

“Don’t come closer,” Mira gasped. “There are pieces of something on the beach.”

Neris looked from Mira to the mound of seaweed. Understanding crossed her face, followed by sorrow.

“Oh, Mira.”

“What are they?”

“Your legs.”

“They can’t be mine. They’re over there.”

Neris lifted the seaweed. Mira felt the touch as if her sister’s fingers were moving across her own skin.

“You are still joined to them,” Neris said gently. “Not in the way you were joined to your tail. The change has made the connection invisible, but it is there.”

Mira stared at the pale limbs. “Put them back.”

“I can help you wear them. I cannot change them into what they were.”

Neris brought the legs to her and arranged them beneath her body. The instant they touched her hips, they became firmly attached. Skin joined skin without seam or scar. Mira kicked in horror, striking her heel against a stone.

Pain burst up her spine.

She curled around herself and wept.

For three days Neris remained with her in a sheltered cave above the tide line. She brought water in shells and gathered berries from the low bushes near the cliffs. Each morning, she taught Mira the names of what had happened to her.

Knees. Ankles. Heels. Toes.

Hunger. Air. Gravity.

Mira hated all of them.

In the sea, movement had begun at the center of her body. A sweep of her tail carried her wherever she wished to go. On land, every motion was divided. One leg had to move while the other remained still. Her feet had to meet the ground at careful angles. Her knees betrayed her without warning. Even sitting required thought.

“Stand,” Neris said on the fourth morning.

Mira gripped a stone ledge and pulled herself upright. The world lurched downward. She had never been so high above the earth. Her legs trembled, and her feet seemed too small to support her.

“I can’t.”

“You are already standing.”

“I am falling.”

“Not yet.”

The moment Neris spoke, Mira’s knees folded. She struck the cave floor and tore the skin from both palms.

“I told you.”

Neris washed the blood away with seawater. “And tomorrow you will fall differently.”

Mira glared at her. “Is that meant to comfort me?”

“No,” Neris said. “It is meant to be true.”

Learning to walk took weeks.

At first Mira could cross the cave only by clinging to the wall. Then she learned to balance with a stick. Later, she managed three steps without help, though the effort left her shaking. Each success carried its own punishment. Her feet blistered. Her muscles cramped at night. Her hips ached as if the bones were still changing inside her.

The land offered no current to hold her. It demanded that she carry her entire weight.

Sometimes she dreamed of swimming. In those dreams, her tail flashed behind her, powerful and whole. She dove through green water and felt the pressure of the deep close around her like an embrace. When she woke, her legs were tangled in blankets, and the silence of the cave seemed unbearable.

She would reach down in the darkness and search for scales.

Once, during a rainstorm, she crawled to the edge of the sea. Neris found her with her legs submerged and her face turned toward the waves.

“If I go far enough,” Mira said, “perhaps they will change back.”

Neris did not answer.

Mira dragged herself deeper. Water rose to her waist, then her chest. For one hopeful moment she felt almost weightless. She pushed away from the rocks and tried to swim as she once had.

Her legs separated.

One kicked upward while the other sank. Her arms thrashed. Salt water filled her mouth. Neris caught her beneath the shoulders and pulled her back to shore.

Mira coughed until her ribs hurt. “The sea doesn’t know me.”

“It knows you,” Neris said.

“Then why did it let me drown?”

“Because knowing you is not the same as making you what you were.”

After that, Mira refused to practice for several days.

She lay facing the cave wall while Neris spoke of inland places: fields where grass moved like shallow water, forests taller than kelp, roads that crossed mountains, cities bright with thousands of lamps. Mira listened despite herself.

“What does walking feel like when it no longer hurts?” she finally asked.

Neris considered. “Like choosing a direction and slowly becoming the person who reaches it.”

Mira turned to look at her. “You have never walked.”

“No,” Neris said. “But I have watched.”

The next morning, Mira stood again.

Summer passed. By autumn she could walk along the shore without a stick. Her steps remained cautious, and sharp stones still punished the soles of her feet, but she began to discover what legs could do.

They could climb.

They could leap, though not gracefully.

They could carry her beyond the line of cliffs that had once marked the edge of her world.

From the highest hill, Mira saw the sea spread below her, vast and blue. She had known its trenches, gardens, caverns, and drowned ruins, yet she had never seen its full shape. Distance transformed it into something both familiar and unreachable.

Neris surfaced in the cove and raised one arm.

Mira waved back.

For a moment, joy lifted inside her. Then she remembered racing beside her sister through forests of coral, their shoulders nearly touching. The joy did not vanish, but grief entered it, and the two feelings remained together.

Years later, Mira would walk farther than she had imagined possible. She would learn roads and cities. She would dance badly, then well. She would discover the pleasure of running downhill and the exhaustion of climbing stone steps. She would wear through many pairs of shoes.

But she never stopped missing her tail.

On cold mornings, pain still lived deep in her hips. In dreams, she remained a creature of the sea. Sometimes she woke mourning not only what she had lost, but also the self who had once believed that change meant exchanging one life neatly for another.

It did not.

Transformation had given her a horizon and taken away a home. It had opened paths before her while closing the depths behind. The new world was beautiful, but its beauty did not repay the old one.

So Mira learned to walk without calling walking a cure.

Each step carried her forward. Each step also pressed the memory of the sea into the earth beneath her feet.
outputs.L5:
She dreamed of places beyond the horizon.  
You encouraged her to take the first step.  
They said the journey would be difficult, but she continued.

Along the way, she discovered courage, you offered hope, and they learned not to underestimate her. In the end, the destination mattered less than the people who helped transform a dream into reality: she, you, and they.

counterfactuals.prompt: Rewrite the moment when the Little Mermaid first wakes up with human legs, using dark humor, Irish vernacular, and a bewildered mermaid who initially thinks the legs are a drunken hospital prank.
counterfactuals.output:
She woke on the strand with a mouthful of sand, a skull full of church bells, and two pale, knobbly things where her tail had been.

For a long moment, she stared at them.

Then one of the things twitched.

“Ah, now,” she whispered. “That’s not funny.”

She sat up too quickly and nearly fainted. The night before returned in damp, miserable scraps: the sea-witch’s cave, a cup of something smoking green, and the witch saying, *This may sting a little*—which was apparently magical language for *You’ll wish your mother had swallowed the egg.*

The mermaid poked one of the new limbs. It bent in the middle.

“Sweet merciful tides.”

There were feet at the ends. Feet. Five toes apiece, lined up like tiny drowned men waiting to identify a body.

Her eyes narrowed.

“This is a hospital prank.”

It had to be. Sailors were forever washing overboard drunk, waking in coastal infirmaries with their eyebrows shaved and rude pictures drawn on their bellies. Clearly, she’d been rescued, sedated, and fitted with some dead woman’s legs for the amusement of cruel medical students.

“Very clever!” she shouted toward the dunes. “Ha-bloody-ha! Now bring back me tail before I report the lot of ye!”

Only gulls answered. One dropped something white and unspeakable beside her hand.

“Grand. Even the staff are hostile.”

She tried to stand.

The legs folded instantly, and she went face-first into the sand.

Pain shot through her as though every bone had been individually introduced to a hammer. She rolled onto her back, gasping, while the waves crept close enough to touch her toes and then retreated, apparently wanting no involvement.

“How do humans use these?” she demanded. “There’s too many joints and not a fin between them. Barbaric design.”

She lifted one foot. The toes wiggled.

She screamed.

The toes stopped.

After a cautious pause, she wiggled them again.

“Oh, that’s vile,” she said, fascinated. “Do it again.”

They did.

Somewhere beyond the dunes came the sound of approaching hooves. The mermaid looked down at her naked, useless new body, then at the gull, which was eyeing her as if considering where to start.

“If this is humanity,” she muttered, dragging herself upright by a rock, “I’d sooner have married a shark. At least they’re honest about eating you.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal literary paragraph about a mermaid discovering that her tail has been replaced by two legs, referring to them as “thingammies” and ending with a melancholy pun about her fallen arches and broken heart.
counterfactuals.output: At dawn the mermaid woke on a beach made of sleeping mirrors and found her silver tail gone, replaced by two pale, jointed thingammies that bent like questions beneath her. She lifted one, then the other, astonished by their toes—ten small prophets pointing inland—while the sea folded and unfolded behind her like a letter it regretted writing. Each step filled her with the impossible weight of gravity, and she wandered toward the city where fountains whispered in her native tongue but refused to answer. By nightfall, the thingammies ached, her footprints had filled with stars, and she understood the sorrow of becoming human: her arches had fallen, and her heart had lost its sole.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Retell a classic fairy-tale transformation scene in a bawdy, modern Irish voice. Set it in a hospital around New Year’s Eve, have a nurse explain how legs work, and blend slapstick comedy with sadness.
counterfactuals.output:
At eleven minutes to midnight on New Year’s Eve, the mermaid woke in St Brigid’s Hospital with two legs, one paper gown, and no earthly notion where her arse had gone.

“Easy now,” said Nurse Bernie, catching her before she slid off the trolley. “You’ve had a major anatomical reshuffle.”

The girl stared down. Where her silver tail had been, there were two pale, bruised-looking limbs ending in ten pink toes. They wriggled independently, like a committee unable to agree on anything.

She opened her mouth. Nothing came out.

“Lost the voice, have we?” Bernie said. “Typical. Men promise you the moon, take your best asset, and leave you with a pair of knees.”

The mermaid pointed wildly at the legs.

“Yes, legs. Standard issue. Hip at the top, foot at the bottom, and the knee in the middle, which is a treacherous little bastard. The basic principle is: one goes forward, then the other. Don’t try both at once unless you’re entering the sack race.”

The mermaid nodded with great seriousness.

“That seriousness won’t last,” said Bernie. “Wait till you meet stairs.”

Outside, fireworks were already being tested over the city, each bang making the windows shiver. Inside, St Brigid’s smelled of disinfectant, boiled cabbage, and the ghost of a thousand cigarettes smoked by men who’d been warned.

Bernie helped her stand.

The mermaid’s knees folded at once. She dropped, caught the curtain, and brought down the entire rail, exposing an elderly man in the next cubicle wearing nothing but compression stockings and the expression of a bishop surprised in a nightclub.

“Happy New Year,” he said.

The mermaid tried again.

“Arse out, shoulders back,” Bernie instructed. “No, not that far out. You’re walking, love, not advertising.”

One foot lifted. Then the other. For three miraculous seconds she moved across the linoleum, upright and human.

Then she stepped on the hem of her gown, flashed half the orthopaedic ward, and landed face-first in a bowl of custard.

There was applause from somewhere near Radiology.

Bernie hauled her up, wiping custard from her eyebrows. “That’s nearly it.”

The girl’s eyes filled.

“Ah,” Bernie said softly. “Here now.”

From beneath the trolley, the mermaid retrieved a small waterproof photograph. In it, beneath green water, an old king with a beard of coral stood among six laughing daughters. All of them had tails. All of them had voices. Behind them, the palace windows glowed gold in the deep.

Bernie looked at the photograph, then at the girl’s new feet.

“So that’s the price.”

The mermaid nodded.

“And himself? The fella you did all this for?”

She pointed toward the window. Across the street, on the giant television over a pub door, a handsome young prince was kissing a woman in a silver dress while the crowd counted down around them.

Ten.

The mermaid pressed both hands to the glass.

Nine.

Bernie’s face tightened. “Oh, the absolute gobshite.”

Eight.

The prince kissed the woman again.

Seven.

The mermaid made a sound then—not a word, because words had been taken, but a small torn noise, like a net ripping underwater.

Six.

Bernie put an arm around her. “Listen to me. Legs aren’t only for chasing fellas.”

Five.

The girl looked at her.

“They’re for leaving them.”

Four.

A firework burst blue over the roofs.

Three.

“They’re for dancing badly, kicking doors open, and walking into places where nobody knows what you gave up.”

Two.

“And occasionally,” Bernie added, “for wearing a skirt so short it causes a minor theological crisis.”

One.

The city exploded in light.

The mermaid laughed without sound. She took one step, then another. Her knees wobbled, her feet slapped the floor, and the back of her gown flapped open like a surrender flag.

The old man in compression stockings raised his paper cup.

“To legs,” he said.

She made it three full paces before crashing into the New Year’s decorations and emerging with a tinsel halo.

Bernie steadied her.

“Perfect,” she said. “You look like every woman who ever made a terrible decision and survived it.”

Beyond the glass, the prince vanished into the cheering crowd.

The mermaid watched until she could no longer tell him from anyone else.

Then she turned—slowly, painfully, magnificently—and walked the other way.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine the Little Mermaid waking after surgery with no understanding of human anatomy. Describe her throwing her unfamiliar legs out of bed, tumbling after them, and slowly realizing they are attached to her.
counterfactuals.output:
She woke beneath a heap of white linen, startled by the strange weight at the end of her body.

Something moved under the blankets.

The Little Mermaid froze. Then, gathering her courage, she seized the coverlet and flung it aside. Two pale, jointed limbs lay where her tail should have been. They looked absurdly separate from her—like a pair of sleeping strangers who had somehow climbed into bed beside her.

She gave an alarmed kick.

Both limbs jerked.

With a gasp, she grabbed one in each hand and heaved them over the side of the bed, determined to be rid of them. They dropped heavily toward the floor.

And took the rest of her with them.

She tumbled after them in a whirl of sheets, landing in an undignified heap. For a moment she lay still, bewildered. Then she lifted her head.

The limbs were still there.

More troublingly, she could feel the cold floor beneath their small, delicate ends. She wiggled one of the tiny projections. A toe moved. She tried another. Then all ten fluttered like pale sea creatures.

Slowly, she touched her hip, traced the line of one leg to the knee, and followed it down to the ankle. Every brush of her fingers answered inside her, faint but unmistakable.

Her eyes widened.

They were not following her.

They were attached to her.

She sat amid the fallen sheets, staring at her new legs with astonishment. Then, very carefully, she bent one knee.

The leg obeyed.

A smile began to spread across her face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a brief experimental monologue narrated in a colloquial Celtic style about a sea-woman receiving legs, with grotesque food imagery, playful counting, irreverent humor, and an ominous closing reflection on the months of painful adjustment.
counterfactuals.output:
Ah now, look at me: two legs, fresh as butcher’s eels and twice as wobbly. One, two—Jesus, there’s knees on them. Three—no, that’s a toe. Ten toes altogether, lined up like boiled grubs on a wedding ham.

The witch says, “Walk.”

“Walk yourself,” says I, for she’s still got a tail and the smugness of a gull stealing chips.

Still, up I heaves. Step one: pudding. Step two: knives. Step three: down I go, face-first into a platter of jellied cod, its dead eye judging my technique.

Grand thing, being human. Your bones grind, your feet blister, and everyone insists on shoes—wee leather coffins with buckles.

I laughed then. I had to.

For the bargain never mentioned the months ahead: each dawn teaching the meat to move, each night salting the sheets red, while far below, the sea kept counting without me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
